claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on cells isolated from 4 mm full-thickness biopsy punches on mouse back skin at 24 hr and 48 hr after injury.
source: To assess cellular and molecular heterogeneity of the wound bed during the inflammatory phase, we performed scRNA-seq on cells isolated from 4 mm full-thickness biopsy punches on mouse back skin at 24 hr and 48 hr after injury (Shook et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental method used to generate the scRNA-seq data.

claim: A 6 mm biopsy punch was used to collect tissue to ensure capture of immediately adjacent tissue and cells that may have migrated into the wound site.
source: To ensure that we also captured the immediately adjacent tissue as well as cells that may have migrated into the wound site, we used a 6 mm biopsy punch to collect the tissue before isolating cells using enzymatic digestion (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design rationale and method.

claim: Four major cell types were classified in the scRNA-seq data: monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells, and fibroblasts at both timepoints.
source: By training a neural network to identify cell types based on expression of established marker genes (as in Wasko et al., 2022; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B), we classified four major cell types in the scRNA-seq data, including monocytes/macrophages (Mono/MO), neutrophils (Neut), dendritic cells (DC), and fibroblasts (FB) at both timepoints (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational analysis method and references figures showing the cell type classifications.

claim: The 24 hr and 48 hr samples clustered separately with minimal overlap, suggesting dramatic changes occurred in the first 2 days of inflammation.
source: Surprisingly, the 24 hr and 48 hr samples clustered separately with minimal overlap, suggesting that dramatic changes occurred in the first 2 days of inflammation (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation from the UMAP plots and provides an interpretation.

claim: The absolute number of macrophages and neutrophils increased >2-fold between 24 hr and 48 hr.
source: The absolute number of macrophages and neutrophils increased >2-fold over this interval (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states a quantitative finding and references a figure.

claim: Approximately 70% of each of the three immune cell populations was collected at 48 hr.
source: While approximately 70% of each of the three immune cell populations was collected at 48 hr, the majority of fibroblasts were found in the 24 hr population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript provides a quantitative observation from the data analysis.

claim: The majority of fibroblasts were found in the 24 hr population.
source: While approximately 70% of each of the three immune cell populations was collected at 48 hr, the majority of fibroblasts were found in the 24 hr population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript provides a quantitative observation from the data analysis.

claim: Genes upregulated by each cell type were markedly different between timepoints.
source: We also found that genes upregulated by each cell type were markedly different between timepoints (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), indicating major changes to expression patterns in the same cell type over time.
evidence: The manuscript describes a finding from differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, and DCs upregulated mRNAs involved in their specific function in inflammation for cytokine production, chemotaxis, and antigen presentation, respectively.
source: Monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, and DCs upregulated mRNAs involved in their specific function in inflammation for cytokine production, chemotaxis, and antigen presentation, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript describes gene ontology analysis results for immune cell types.

claim: Fibroblasts uniquely upregulated genes involved in extracellular matrix (ECM) organization.
source: Similarly, fibroblasts uniquely upregulated genes involved in extracellular matrix (ECM) organization.
evidence: The manuscript describes gene ontology analysis results for fibroblasts.

claim: DCs, fibroblasts, and neutrophils upregulated genes involved in apoptosis and cell death.
source: Interestingly, DCs, fibroblasts, and neutrophils upregulated genes involved in apoptosis and cell death (Figure 1F and G).

claim: Neutrophils upregulated the largest number of mRNAs for apoptosis including Casp3, S100a8, and S100a9.
source: Neutrophils upregulated the largest number of mRNAs for apoptosis including Casp3, which is cleaved to activate apoptosis, and S100a8 and S100a9, which induce apoptosis of several cell types (Yui et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript describes specific genes upregulated in neutrophils and cites a reference for their function.

claim: S100a8 and S100a9 induce apoptosis of several cell types.

source: Overall, these data suggest that apoptosis occurs during inflammation after skin injury.

claim: Gas6 was highly expressed by a specific subset of monocyte/macrophage cells that also overexpressed Lyve1, Timd4, and Retnla.
source: Examining the UMAP plot to determine the heterogeneity of efferocytosis gene expression within individual cell types, we observed that Gas6 was highly expressed by a specific subset of monocyte/macrophage cells. These cells also overexpressed the resident macrophage marker Lyve1, the apoptosis receptor Timd4, and Retnla, a downstream factor of efferocytosis (Figure 2B), indicating that they may play a role in apoptosis detection and response in wound healing.

claim: Lyve1 has been identified as a marker for resident macrophages, which are distinct from the majority of wound macrophages that differentiate from bone marrow-derived monocytes and are recruited to the wound after injury.

claim: Lyve1+ cells in wound beds are resident rather than recruited to the wound bed after injury.

claim: Lyve1+ cells co-expressed Gas6 protein.
source: Further, we confirmed that Lyve1+ cells co-expressed Gas6 protein (Figure 2D) and that Timd4 protein (Figure 2E) was expressed in wound beds.

claim: The TAM receptor Axl was uniquely expressed in the single-cell dataset by both dendritic cells and fibroblasts.
source: The TAM receptor Axl was uniquely expressed in the single-cell dataset by both dendritic cells and fibroblasts (Figure 2A).

claim: Axl expression was confirmed in 24 hr wound beds in both dendritic cells (CD11c) and fibroblasts (Pdgfra-GFP).

claim: Fibroblasts displayed elongated GFP+ processes with central localization of Axl.
source: Using immunofluorescence staining, we confirmed Axl expression in 24 hr wound beds in both dendritic cells (CD11c) (Figure 2F) and fibroblasts (Pdgfra-GFP) (Figure 2G), which displayed elongated GFP+ processes with central localization of Axl.

claim: The ligand Gas6 was significantly downregulated in wound beds compared to naive skin.
source: All efferocytosis receptor mRNAs studied, including the TAM receptors, were significantly upregulated in the wound bed compared to naive skin, while the ligand Gas6 was significantly downregulated.

claim: Socs1 and Socs3 were significantly upregulated in wound beds compared to naive skin.

source: Additional studies have shown that hypoxic environments (such as those found in diabetic wounds) increase macrophage efferocytosis (Wang et al., 2023), though other studies have indicated that macrophage efferocytosis is defective in diabetic wounds (Khanna et al., 2010).

source: Additional studies have shown that hypoxic environments (such as those found in diabetic wounds) increase macrophage efferocytosis (Wang et al., 2023), though other studies have indicated that macrophage efferocytosis is defective in diabetic wounds (Khanna et al., 2010).

claim: Several alterations in the expression of mRNAs associated with apoptotic signaling pathways were found between non-diabetic and diabetic foot ulcers.

claim: The anti-Axl Ab treatment reduced Axl signaling in skin wounds.
